L180: Our approach consisted of defining the learning component of any individual decision-making trajectories as the predictive mean under our model (【66†Fig. 3a】-left). This is obtained by updating the weights ${\mathbf{w}}_{t}$ using the learning rule in 【46†eq. 2】 with the animal’s decisions ${\mathsf{y}}_{t}$, without any noise. The noise component of the dynamics is then taken to be the residual between the posterior mean (the “inferred” trajectory) and learning component (【66†Fig. 3a】).
L181: We plot in 【66†Fig. 3b】 the resulting learning and inferred trajectories overlaid for an example mouse, reflecting a high-degree of alignment and capturing some of the idiosyncrasies of the learning dynamics of this particular mouse. The learning decompositions for all three example mice can be found in 【68†Appendix C.2】, and we plot in 【66†Fig. 3c】 the learning and posterior trajectories, averaging over the $N=31$ animals considered. Finally, we found (【66†Fig.
L182: 3d】) this definition of the noise component to match the inferred parameter values of noise scale $\sigma $ per animal with high correlation $(\rho =0.79)$, providing support for this learning decomposition as consistent with our modeling.
L183: We found the learning component to recapitulate the key learning weight dynamics of the inferred posterior mean, such as the primary side dominance and even the trial-to-trial “noisy” fluctuation in weights and bias. To quantify how much the learning component accounts for the inferred weights trajectory on every trial we considered the learning fraction (【66†Fig.
L184: 3a】-right), defined as the ratio between the norm of the learning update $\alpha \cdot {ℒ}_{\varphi }({\mathbf{w}}_{t};{\mathsf{y}}_{t},{\mathit{x}}_{t})$ and the norm of the residual noise with the inferred weight update ${\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{t+1}-{\widehat{\mathbf{w}}}_{t}$ (【66†Fig. 3e】-left), averaged over all trials. For reference, a noise-only model like PsyTrack [【33†16】] has a learning fraction of strictly 0, and a deterministic learning-only model 1.
L185: We include in 【68†Appendix C.2】 alternate metrics, such as projection fraction, cosine similarity and the one considered in previous work [【52†22】]—we found no qualitative difference. We found the vector PG accounted for significantly more of the learning component (【66†Fig.3e】) than the scalar version, as a distribution over individual animals. This learning fraction was consistently higher across regressors considered, with the largest difference being for the bias (【66†Fig. 3f】).
L186: This supports our inferred model as an appropriate mechanistic model, able to generate and recapitulate the learning dynamics observed empirically.
L187: ### 2.4. Dynamic learning rate
L188: So far, the learning rate $\alpha $ governing the learning dynamics has been static, optimized as a hyperparameter with MLE. This assumes the learning rule is engaged with equally over learning; a restrictive assumption richly studied [【69†31】], with further recent work [【70†17】, 【34†18】] pointing to the contrary through nonstationarity in internal states over learning. To provide a dynamic generalization of our learning model, we placed a random-walk prior on the learning rate as
L189: $${\alpha }_{t+1}={\alpha }_{t}+{\omega }_{t}$$  | (10a)
L190: $${\mathbf{w}}_{t+1}={\mathbf{w}}_{t}+{\alpha }_{t}\cdot {ℒ}_{\varphi }({\mathbf{w}}_{t};{\mathit{x}}_{t},{\mathsf{y}}_{t})+{ϵ}_{t}$$  | (10b)
L191: with ${\omega }_{t}\sim 𝒩(0,{\sigma }_{\alpha }^{2})$ and initial condition ${\alpha }_{1}\sim 𝒩({\alpha }_{0},{\sigma }_{\alpha }^{2})$, with ${\mathbf{w}}_{1}$ and ${\{{ϵ}_{t}\}}_{t=1}^{T}$ sampled as in the static case. The learning rule ${ℒ}_{\varphi }$ is taken to be exactly the vector PG update in 【63†(9)】, including a global learning rate parameter $\alpha $ dynamically scaled by the latent variable ${\alpha }_{t}$—this dynamic PG model of 【71†eqs.
L192: 10】 thus encompasses strictly the vector PG model, with additional $\{{\alpha }_{0},{\sigma }_{\alpha }\}$ scalar parameters. The learning rate is now a dynamic latent variable that is fully integrated out (alongside the weights) in computing the marginal log-likelihood, and for which we can compute posterior trajectories over trials $t$. This learning rate acts as a latent gating on the learning signal, dictating how much an animal engages with a certain learning rule on trial $t$.
L193: We found mice to show a dynamic learning rate, which in turn helped predicting the learning component. First, we plot in 【72†Fig.
L194: 4a】 the difference $\mathrm{log}\phantom{\rule{thinmathspace}{0ex}}{\widehat{\alpha }}_{t}-\mathrm{log}\phantom{\rule{thinmathspace}{0ex}}{\widehat{\alpha }}_{1}$ over learning for the per-animal posterior learning rate ${\widehat{\alpha }}_{1:T}$; since the dynamical learning rate ${\widehat{\alpha }}_{t}$ scales a static parameter $\alpha $, we use the difference in log values which is invariant to such scaling.
L195: We found highly dynamic learning rate trajectories in the inferred posterior mean for ${\widehat{\alpha }}_{1:T}$, differing across individuals (【72†Fig. 4a】). Now, we can use this inferred learning rates to refine our prediction the learning component (【41†§2.3】) of the trajectory, using the inferred ${\widehat{\alpha }}_{t}$ at every time step $t$ of the predictive trajectory. We found this to help the learning component more closely match the inferred trajectory (【72†Fig.
L196: 4b】), and generally lead to an increase in the learning fraction (【72†Fig. 4c】) over animals. The dynamic PG model did provide an increase in marginal log-likelihood over animals (【72†Fig. 4d】), which includes the held-out test trials attesting to an increase in quality of fit.

L431: ### C.3. Weight non-identifiability in GLM likelihood
L432: 
L433: Here we discuss weight $\mathbf{w}$ identifiability considerations for the Bernoulli GLM policy model considered so far. We define weights ${\mathbf{w}}_{1}$ and ${\mathbf{w}}_{2}$ to be non-identifiable on the basis of a function $f$, like the likelihood, if $f({\mathbf{w}}_{1})=f({\mathbf{w}}_{2})$.
L434: Consider the Bernoulli GLM policy studied so far, with left and right stimulus intensities ${x}_{L}$ and ${x}_{R}$ vectorized into $\mathit{x}=[{x}_{L},{x}_{R},1]$ and weights $\mathbf{w}=[{w}_{L},{w}_{R},b]$,
L435: 
L436: $$p(\mathsf{y}\phantom{\rule{thinmathspace}{0ex}}\mid \phantom{\rule{thinmathspace}{0ex}}\mathbf{w},\mathit{x})=\sigma (\mathsf{y}\cdot {\mathbf{w}}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathit{x})=\sigma (\mathsf{y}\cdot ({w}_{L}{x}_{L}+{w}_{R}{x}_{R}+b))$$  | (30)
L437: for $\mathsf{y}\in \{-1,1\}$. Now, consider the following perturbation
L438: 
L439: $$[{w}_{L},{w}_{R},b]\mapsto [{w}_{L}+ϵ,{w}_{R}+ϵ,b-ϵ]$$  | (31)
L440: 
L441: for $ϵ>0$. We will show that this kind of perturbation has minimal to no effect on the likelihood, but can have a substantial effect on the evolution of the weights. Indeed, let $f(ϵ;\mathbf{w},\mathit{x})$ be the likelihood of $\mathsf{y}=R$ with this perturbation
L442: $$f(ϵ;\mathbf{w},\mathit{x})=p(y=R\phantom{\rule{thinmathspace}{0ex}}\mid \phantom{\rule{thinmathspace}{0ex}}[w+ϵ,b-ϵ],\mathit{x})=\sigma (({w}_{L}+ϵ){x}_{L}+({w}_{R}+ϵ){x}_{R}+b-ϵ).$$  | (32)
L443: 
L444: We can examine the influence of $ϵ$ on $f$ through it’s impact on the derivative. It is easy to see that
L445: 
L446: $$\frac{\partial }{\partial ϵ}f(ϵ;\mathbf{w},\mathit{x})=f(ϵ;\mathbf{w},\mathit{x})(1-f(ϵ;\mathbf{w},\mathit{x}))({x}_{L}+{x}_{R}-1).$$  | (33)
L447: 
L448: from which we can conclude a few things
L449:   * If either ${x}_{L}=1$ or ${x}_{R}=1$, ${\scriptstyle \frac{\partial }{\partial ϵ}}f(ϵ;\mathbf{w},\mathit{x})=0$ meaning that this kind of perturbation would have no impact on the log-lik;
L450: 
L451:   * As $ϵ$ increases, ${\scriptstyle \frac{\partial }{\partial ϵ}}f(ϵ;\mathbf{w},\mathit{x})\to 0$ meaning it has less and less of an impact on the log-lik;
L452: 
L453: see 【93†Fig. 8a】 for a heatmap of ${\scriptstyle \frac{\partial }{\partial ϵ}}f$ over $\{s,ϵ\}$ for $s={x}_{R}-{x}_{L}$ the stimulus intensity.
L454: This creates a “weak” form of non-identifiability where substantial changes in the weights, or parameters, will have small (non-zero) changes in the log-likelihood, becoming strict at the boundary $\mid s\mid =1$ We noticed this behavior in Psytrack – see an example below in 【93†Fig. 8c】. We elect thus to fix the bias term to 0 until contrast of sufficiently low-levels have been observed in the data.

L910: ## Appendix C Additional details on model and data
L911: 
L912: Simulated data. We simulate a pool of animals, each following the same underlying learning rule. In Supp. Fig. 【65†11】, we also explore populations with mixed weight update functions, where pooling tends to recover an in-between weight update function. Even when animals follow the same rule, their learning trajectories differ due to the stochasticity of received inputs and behavior.
L913: For each simulated animal, the learning process unfolds over trials $t=0,1,\dots,T$ as follows. Each stimulus $s_{t}$ is drawn uniformly from discrete values in $[-2,2]$ with 0.25 increments, excluding 0 (except for Fig. 【50†2】, which includes 0); varying the increment size did not affect our conclusions. The correct label or answer is defined as $z_{t}=\mathbbm{1}[s_{t}>0]$.
L914: Decision weights are updated according to $\mathbf{w}_{t+1}=\mathbf{w}_{t}+\Delta\mathbf{w}_{t}$, where $\Delta\mathbf{w}_{t}$ is computed from the ground-truth learning rule being tested (see Supp.  【14†B】). The agent’s binary choice $y_{t}\in\{0,1\}$ is sampled from a Bernoulli GLM parameterized by $\mathbf{w}_{t}$, as described in Section 【7†2】. A reward is given if the choice matches the correct answer: $r_{t}=\mathbbm{1}[y_{t}=z_{t}]$.
L915: For the total number of trials $T$, we use $T=500$ by default (to speed up simulations), but also demonstrate that our conclusions hold for longer $T$ ($T=8000$) in Supp. Fig. 【67†10】. We set the learning rate $\alpha$ such that the animal’s performance reaches a saturation regime — typically when the stimulus weight approaches a value of $3$ for this task.
L916: The GLM includes a stimulus weight that is updated over trials, and a fixed bias weight sampled randomly at the start of each simulation from $\{-1,0,1\}$. We simulate a pool of 10 to 1000 animals to observe the influence of data availability on reconstruction accuracy in Fig. 【50†2】C. We evaluate model performance using 5-fold cross-validation, where each fold holds out a subset of animals entirely.
L917: This ensures generalization across individuals, consistent with the underlying assumption of pooling — that animals share commonalities which can be learned from a subset and applied to held-out animals.
L918: IBL data. We use the publicly available International Brain Laboratory (IBL) dataset [【56†31】], and follow the same preprocessing pipeline as [【38†19】], with details available in their accompanying code. For dataset details and learning curves, refer to Supp. C and Fig. S1 in [【38†19】]. In other words, we used the same preprocessed dataset as [【38†19】] ($N=12$), for benchmarking purposes. For evaluation, we adopt two cross-validation strategies, and both led to similar trends (Tables 【73†1】 and 【74†2】).
L919: First, under the pooling assumption that a shared learning model generalizes across animals, we use $K$-fold cross-validation with animal-held-out splits. We fit the model using the first 10000 trials per animal to capture the full learning trajectory, including the saturation phase. For each fold, we report the average validation log-likelihood across four random seeds and conduct paired $t$-tests across matched animals to obtain the $p$-values reported in Table 【73†1】.
L920: The paired design accounts for variability in individual animals’ performance: animals who learn well are easier to predict, while animals who have not learned the task are harder to model (see Fig. S1 in [【38†19】]). Second, to assess temporal generalization, we adopt a future-data holdout strategy [【190†107】]. We train up to the point where the learning curve inflects (around trial 5500), ensuring that the evaluation data reflect ongoing learning rather than the saturation regime.
L921: This also avoids cutting off training too early, where little learning signals are present. We then evaluate performance on the next 500 trials beyond that point, although similar trends were observed when using 200 or 1000 trials instead. As above, we compute paired $t$-tests on animal-matched log-likelihoods to assess significance.
L922: Learning model, initial GLM weights, and hyperparameters. Our learning rule model is depicted in Fig. 【49†1】C. The network takes as input the current trial stimulus $s_{t}$, choice $y_{t}$, reward $r_{t}$, and the current weight $\mathbf{w}_{t}$. For the IBL data, we additionally include binary inputs indicating daybreak and stimulus side; the trends in Table 【73†1】 remain unchanged when these inputs are omitted. The network then outputs inferred weight update.
L923: For choice and reward, we input the animal’s actual choice and reward rather than those generated by the model, since these are the signals the animal would have access to when updating its weights; this approach is also consistent with previous studies. The DNN architecture consists of two hidden layers with 32 units each, while the RNN uses a single recurrent layer with 32 hidden units.
L924: All architectural components and training settings are treated as hyperparameters and tuned via cross-validation by animal held-out. All neural network weights and biases were treated as trainable parameters.
L925: To estimate the initial decision weights $\mathbf{w}_{0}$, we treat them as trainable parameters but initialize them using a psychometric curve fit to the first 100 trials. Specifically, we compute the empirical probability of choosing $y=1$ as a function of stimulus value, which defines a psychometric curve.
L926: Since we model the choice probability as $\sigma(\mathbf{w}^{\top}x)$, where $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid, we apply the inverse-sigmoid (logit) transformation to the empirical probabilities, yielding a linear target $b=\text{logit}(p(y=1|x))$. We then fit $\mathbf{w}_{0}$ via a least-squares regression to the equation $\mathbf{w}^{\top}x=b$ using the stimulus values. We investigate the sensitivity of performance to incorrect $\mathbf{w}_{0}$ in Table 【68†5】.
L927: As mentioned, to enable faster simulations and repeated robustness tests, we used shorter trial sequences. Because these provide fewer early samples, we initialized with a known initial weight. That said, applying our method to unknown initial weight still led to accurate recovery (Supp. Fig. 【67†10】).
L928: For IBL data, however, we instead initialize $\mathbf{w}_{0}=\vec{0}$, following [【38†19】], since animals typically start at chance-level performance; we also verified that training $\mathbf{w}_{0}$ did not significantly impact our results on IBL data.
L929: We tune hyperparameters, including the number of hidden units, number of layers, learning rate, and number of training epochs. We used a batch size of 1 for simulated data. For real IBL data, we trained on all animals jointly; using a batch size of 1 instead did not affect our conclusions.
L930: Cross-validation ensures generalization and helps mitigate overfitting, in addition to the fact that neural networks in feature learning regime inherently favor smooth function approximators via implicit regularization (see Discussion). These implicit biases are themselves controlled by architectural choices and training regimes (e.g., depth, width, and training duration) [【131†88】, 【191†108】], which justifies the need for hyperparameter tuning.
